value.overview: The Fork-tailed Flycatcher is a striking tyrant flycatcher named for the extremely long, deeply forked tail of adults, especially males. It is usually seen in open country, where it perches conspicuously on wires, fences, shrubs, or isolated trees and launches into the air to catch insects. The species occurs from southern Mexico through much of South America. In Costa Rica, it is most characteristic of the southern Pacific lowlands and foothills.
value.classification: The Fork-tailed Flycatcher belongs to the family Tyrannidae, the tyrant flycatchers, and the genus Tyrannus, which includes kingbirds and related large flycatchers. Several geographically distinct subspecies are recognized, with Central American birds generally sedentary or only locally mobile.
value.identification: Adults have a black head, pale gray upperparts, whitish underparts, and a dark tail with very long outer feathers forming a pronounced fork. The wings are dark, and the bill and legs are black. Juveniles resemble adults but have shorter tails and less sharply defined plumage. Its combination of a long forked tail, gray body, black head, and open-country habits makes it difficult to confuse with other Costa Rican flycatchers.
value.rangeHabitat: The species ranges from southern Mexico and Central America across much of South America to Argentina and Uruguay. In Costa Rica it is a resident, locally common species, especially in the Térraba region and other parts of the southern Pacific slope, generally at about 100–520 meters elevation. It favors savannas, pastures, agricultural landscapes, open woodland, forest edges, river margins, seasonally wet grasslands, and other open habitats with scattered perches. It usually avoids extensive closed forest.
value.migrationStatus: Fork-tailed Flycatchers in Costa Rica are generally resident, particularly the Central American populations, rather than regular long-distance migrants. The species as a whole has contrasting strategies: some South American populations migrate seasonally, while northern populations are mostly sedentary. Costa Rican birds may make local or seasonal movements, and occasional individuals outside the usual range may represent wandering birds.
value.breeding: In Costa Rica, the species breeds in open lowland and foothill habitats, especially where scattered trees, shrubs, or human structures provide nesting sites and nearby grassland or pasture offers feeding areas. The nest is a small cup constructed in a tree or shrub, and both adults participate in territorial defense and care of the young. Breeding timing can vary regionally, but activity is associated with the local rainy-season cycle and periods of plentiful insect prey.
value.dietFeeding: The Fork-tailed Flycatcher feeds mainly on flying insects, including beetles, grasshoppers, wasps, bees, moths, and other aerial prey. It typically waits on an exposed perch and makes fast, acrobatic sallies to capture insects in the air, often returning to the same perch. It may also take prey from vegetation or the ground and occasionally consumes small fruits, especially when insect food is less available.
value.behavior: This is a conspicuous, agile, and strongly aerial flycatcher. It often sits upright on wires, fence posts, treetops, or bare branches, using its long tail to make sharp turns during pursuit. Individuals may occur alone, in pairs, or in small family groups. Breeding birds defend territories and can aggressively chase intruders and predators. Outside the breeding season, larger temporary gatherings may form where food is abundant.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population trend is not considered to be declining at a rate that approaches a threatened-category threshold, although regional trends may differ and detailed monitoring is limited.
